claim_checks.claim: `private` and `protected` are enforced only during type checking. Runtime lookups, and bracket notation even during type checking, still reach the member: it is "soft private".
claim_checks.page_says: private and protected are only enforced during type checking. … private also allows access using bracket notation during type checking. … these fields are soft private
claim_checks.note: Type-check-only enforcement and runtime access are stated for both modifiers. The bracket-notation escape and the "soft private" label are stated for `private` only; the claim's "the member" follows "private and protected", so it widens both to `protected`.

claim_checks.claim: `#` fields stay private after compilation and have no bracket-notation escape hatch: they are "hard private".
claim_checks.page_says: JavaScript’s private fields (#) remain private after compilation and do not provide the previously mentioned escape hatches like bracket notation access, making them hard private.

claim_checks.claim: When compiling to ES2021 or lower, TypeScript replaces `#` with `WeakMap`s. The handbook notes that these runtime privacy checks could affect performance.
claim_checks.page_says: When compiling to ES2021 or less, TypeScript will use WeakMaps in place of #. … Note that these added privacy checks during runtime could affect performance.
claim_checks.note: The handbook's performance note covers WeakMaps, so the narrower claim holds. The same note also names closures and native private fields; see the Summary violation.

claim_checks.claim: Private elements are not properties. They cannot be enumerated, deleted, proxied, or reached through `Object` methods, and `structuredClone()` does not copy them.
claim_checks.page_says: but private elements have none. While private elements are accessed with the familiar dot notation, they cannot be proxied, enumerated, deleted, or interacted with using any Object method.
claim_checks.note: structuredClone part: "structuredClone() does not clone private elements" (same page, Description section).

claim_checks.claim: Reading a `#` field from an object whose class did not declare it throws a `TypeError`. `#x in obj` checks for it without throwing.
claim_checks.page_says: If you access a private element from an object that doesn't have the element, a TypeError is thrown … return true if the private field or method exists, and false otherwise
claim_checks.note: The claim's wording matches the TypeError message the page prints: "Cannot read private member #x from an object whose class did not declare it".

claim_checks.claim: V8 9.7 moved class-field initialization, including private fields, onto its inline-cache fast path. Before that it went through slower runtime calls.
claim_checks.page_says: when V8 considers the pattern of the initialization to be predictable enough, it uses a new IC to speed up the operation … it falls back to a runtime call
claim_checks.note: The "before 9.7" half holds ("V8 always used a costly runtime call"). The claim drops the condition: the IC fast path is used only for predictable initialization patterns, and V8 falls back to the runtime for unseen patterns, proxy targets or fields that already exist.

claim_checks.claim: Private elements cannot be proxied (row: Object wrapped in a Proxy; `#` access does not go through the proxy).
claim_checks.page_says: they cannot be proxied, enumerated, deleted, or interacted with using any Object method.

claim_checks.claim: TypeScript downlevels it (row: Target ES2021 or lower; `#` becomes `WeakMap` lookups).
claim_checks.page_says: When compiling to ES2021 or less, TypeScript will use WeakMaps in place of #.

claim_checks.claim: So code meant to run unbuilt keeps injected collaborators as `readonly #field`s assigned in the constructor (row: working around it with `--experimental-transform-types`; runs on Node 24.22 with an ExperimentalWarning; flag removed in Node 26.0.0).
claim_checks.page_says: Removed --experimental-transform-types flag. … any TypeScript features that involve replacing TypeScript syntax with new JavaScript syntax will error. … parameter properties
claim_checks.note: The premises are on the page: the flag was removed in v26.0.0, and parameter properties fail under type stripping. The ✅-marked conclusion (use `readonly #` fields) is not on the page and does not follow from it: a plain field declaration assigned in the constructor would also strip. The Node 24.22 ExperimentalWarning is a local re-test; the cached page is the v26.13.1 docs and does not mention it.

claim_checks.claim: Node only deletes types (row: type stripping stable since 24.12.0 and 25.2.0; no warning since 24.3.0; ignores tsconfig.json; needs .ts extensions in relative imports).
claim_checks.page_says: Since Node.js is only removing inline types … Node.js will replace TypeScript syntax with whitespace … Node.js ignores tsconfig.json files
claim_checks.note: Context cells match the page: the history table gives stable in v25.2.0 and v24.12.0 and Stability 2, the experimental warning dropped in v24.3.0, and mandatory file extensions in import statements.

violations.evidence: C1: [^1] gives bracket-notation access during type checking and the "soft private" label for `private` only; the claim extends them to `protected`.

C6: [^3] says the 9.7 IC is used "when V8 considers the pattern of the initialization to be predictable enough" and otherwise "falls back to a runtime call"; the claim states the move as unconditional.
C9: [^4] backs the flag's removal in v26.0.0 and the parameter-property error, but not the ✅-marked recommendation to use `readonly #` fields.

The headline "On a native ES2022+ target, reading and creating `#` fields costs the same as public fields" has no mark and no citation, yet Verification status reports 0 unverified claims. Its only evidence is one local run (Node 24.22, V8 13.6) and [^3], which covers initialization only, in V8 ≥ 9.7, with runtime fallbacks. [^1] (rank 1) says runtime privacy checks, private fields included, "could affect performance". This is a hedge, not a contradiction, so it is no KB-17 failure. Takeaways line 2 ("measured cost is nil") repeats the same generalization. Outside the factual_grounding count, since it carries no ✅.

The "Where each form fits" table is decision guidance, not mechanism, so it belongs with role-6 trade-offs. Its row claim "TypeScript error TS18009" has no mark and no citation, and no cached page contains it.
